analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly, fills the coverage gap, and allows cheaper drug imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral and died at the end of the 108th Congress without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug law created a new prescription benefit run through private insurance plans, and it included a clause forbidding the government from negotiating drug prices directly with manufacturers, while keeping imports of cheaper Canadian drugs largely off-limits. This bill would undo all three: it lets the Health and Human Services Secretary bargain on behalf of the roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries the way the VA already does, removes the gap in coverage that forces seniors to pay the full cost of their drugs for part of each year, and legalizes reimportation of prescription drugs from Canada with anti-counterfeiting packaging rules. It was introduced by a single Democrat in June 2004 and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, mostly seniors and people with disabilities, would benefit from lower negotiated drug prices, an end to the coverage gap that leaves them paying full price mid-year, and legal access to lower-priced medicines from Canada. Taxpayers could also benefit if the government's bargaining power lowers what Medicare pays overall.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision in the 2003 Medicare drug law that bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating with drug manufacturers, giving the Secretary the same bulk-purchasing authority the VA and Defense Department already use to get lower prices.
Eliminates the gap in Medicare's drug benefit — the 'donut hole' — and the initial coverage limit, so beneficiaries would no longer have to pay full cost for part of each year.

Legalizes reimportation of prescription drugs from Canada, and extends the right to import to individual consumers, not just pharmacists and wholesalers, with counterfeit-resistant packaging requirements to protect safety.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the main cost through lower prices on Medicare drugs and competition from Canadian imports. Private drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers would lose their exclusive role as price negotiators under the 2003 law. The federal government would cover the expanded drug benefit unless the negotiation savings offset it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and drug plans

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the coverage gap and the initial coverage limit without any dedicated funding source, so the added drug benefit would increase federal spending unless offset elsewhere.

The importation title loosens safety oversight: it removes the requirement for testing by non-wholesaler importers, so individual and pharmacist importers could bring in drugs without the tests wholesalers must run, relying instead on counterfeit-resistant packaging to catch fakes.

Drug makers and private plans argued that government negotiation and bulk importation could reduce manufacturer revenues and, they claimed, future investment in new medicines — the objection an honest supporter would have to answer.
Shifting pricing power from private drug plans to the Secretary of Health and Human Services would concentrate decisions about covered drugs and prices in one federal office.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were large and concrete: lower drug prices for tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries through negotiating power like other federal agencies already use, an end to the coverage gap that forces seniors to pay full price for part of the year, and legal access to cheaper medicines from Canada. The main costs are real but manageable: expanded coverage and gap elimination would add federal spending with no funding source shown in the bill, and the importation title relaxes some testing safeguards even as it adds anti-counterfeiting packaging requirements. On balance, the bill's gains for beneficiaries outweigh its drawbacks, though its total absence of cosponsors suggests it was written more as a statement of principles than a bill built to pass.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on June 3, 2004, the day it was introduced.
Within two weeks it was referred to the health subcommittees of both committees, where it stayed; no markup, hearing, or floor action followed.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with no bipartisan base to push it forward.
The bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, leaving the 2003 law's ban on Medicare price negotiation and its importation restrictions in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and the private drug plans that run Medicare's benefit came out ahead: the ban on government price negotiation and the limits on importing cheaper Canadian drugs stayed on the books for years after this bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Medicare drug plans

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured no cosponsors during its life.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 3, 2004 and never reported the bill or scheduled action on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 3, 2004 and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; the only support on record was a single Democrat and no cosponsor from either party.

industries.note: The bill repeals the provision in the 2003 Medicare drug law that forbids the government from negotiating prices, and reopens the border to cheaper drugs from Canada. Both cut directly into what manufacturers can charge, which is why their interest ran against the bill even as beneficiaries' interest ran for it.

industries.industry: Private drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The 2003 law was built so that private plans, not Medicare, run the drug benefit and bargain with manufacturers. This bill hands that bargaining power to the Secretary of Health and Human Services instead, shrinking the plans' gatekeeping role and the margin that comes with it.
Legal reimportation would create a legal channel for pharmacies, wholesalers, and individual consumers to buy lower-priced drugs from Canada, restoring access that the 2003 law effectively blocked.
